articles.title: How the UK’s net migration figure hit its target after years of government promises
articles.author: Ben Brindle, Senior Researcher, Migration Observatory, University of Oxford
paras: In January 2010, ahead of the general election, then-prime minister David Cameron pledged to bring net migration down to the “tens of thousands” a year. Neither Cameron nor his successor, Theresa May, managed it.

Net migration – the number of people moving to the UK minus those leaving – averaged around 250,000 during the 2010s. It never dropped below 100,000, except for a brief period during 2020 after COVID put a sudden stop to people moving around the world.

That was until the year ending June 2026, when net migration fell to 77,000. This was the lowest level (outside of the pandemic) since 1997. What makes the milestone particularly remarkable is that just three years ago, net migration stood at a historic high of 944,000. Since then, it has plummeted by 92%.
So why have the numbers fallen, and are these low levels here to stay?
The main reason for the decline is lower immigration into the UK. But understanding which government is responsible depends on the period you’re looking at.

The previous Conservative government is largely responsible for both the increase and the initial decrease in net migration. Under Boris Johnson, it liberalised the immigration system after Brexit, reintroducing post-study work visas for international students, opening humanitarian routes for Ukrainians and Hong Kongers, and making care workers eligible for work visas.

But as net migration reached record levels, Rishi Sunak’s government introduced a suite of policies to restrict immigration. These included a ban on care workers and most international students bringing their family members, as well as increased scrutiny of applications to hire migrant care workers.
The restrictions led to a sharp decline in immigration – but largely because immigration had been so high.

Labour introduced further restrictions in 2025, most notably closing the care route to overseas workers. It also announced tighter rules for universities sponsoring international students. This may have made institutions more cautious about offering places, even before the changes took effect in June this year.
These changes have driven the decline over the past year, but have had a smaller impact because net migration was already much lower when Labour entered office.

One reason recent government policies have been more effective at reducing immigration than those of the 2010s is that Brexit gave policymakers greater control over arrivals. Under free movement, EU citizens could move to the UK without a visa, limiting successive governments’ ability to restrict immigration from the bloc. Now, the government can restrict arrivals from any country, particularly those coming for work or study.

Immigration is only one part of the story. High levels of emigration have also helped bring the net figure below 100,000. Much of this is a legacy of the post-pandemic boom, because many migrants – particularly students and workers – stay in the UK for only a few years. In other words, many of those who arrived during the recent period of record immigration are now leaving.
EU citizens who arrived under free movement also contributed to the emigration figures.

The previous government is therefore largely responsible for today’s high emigration figures. This is not because of its restrictive policies, but due to its more liberal policies a few years earlier.

The number of UK citizens leaving the country has also attracted attention. Recent figures are substantially higher than those for the 2010s. But this is not the result of a sudden exodus – instead, in 2021 the Office for National Statistics changed how it estimates British emigration. This has not only increased the emigration estimates, reducing the net migration figure by tens of thousands, but it also means comparisons with the 2010s are unreliable.

In fact, some British emigrants may be people who originally moved to the UK from the EU under free movement and subsequently acquired UK citizenship. It is unclear how many people this applies to, however. Data from the UN show that between 2020 and 2024, Poland, Malta and Romania saw the largest increases in their UK populations. Some may have also been joined by UK-born partners and children.
Will net migration stay this low?

Looking ahead, low net migration will not necessarily represent a new normal. The UK is experiencing an unusual combination of falling immigration and relatively high emigration. This could even push net migration down further next year, as recent visa figures suggest immigration has further to fall.

But the downward pressure from emigration is unlikely to last forever. Since fewer migrants are arriving, fewer will leave in the years ahead. As a result, emigration is likely to fall, which would push net migration back up even if immigration remains at its current level.

After more than a decade of governments trying and failing to bring net migration down, the UK has finally reached Cameron’s infamous target. But some pretty specific circumstances have made that possible, and they will not all be in place forever.

articles.title: We’ve documented almost 1,000 years lost to wrongful convictions across Europe – and we’re still counting
articles.author: Jennifer Maria Schell-Leugers, Associate Professor of Legal Psychology, Maastricht University
paras: It was a cold October night in 2001 when Rudolf Rupp, a 52-year-old farmer from a small town in Bavaria, Germany, vanished. He had gone out drinking at a local bar, as he often did, and never came home. His wife reported him missing, but no one could find a trace of him or his car. For almost two years, it was as if he had just vanished into thin air. No clues, no body. Just silence.

Neighbours gossiped that something terrible had happened at the farm – and that Rupp’s family had killed him. The police began to suspect his wife, two teenage daughters, and the boyfriend of one of the girls. All four eventually confessed.

The story they told was gruesome: that Rudolf had been ambushed, beaten to death, cut into pieces, and disposed of by feeding him to the farm dogs. The case, especially the grisly details of the confessions, drew nationwide media attention in Germany.

But soon after, they took it all back, saying they had been pressured by investigators and that their confessions were not true. They all had intellectual disabilities, and they said they were coerced by police.

In 2005, despite the fact that no body or any type of evidence was found, they were convicted based solely on those confessions. Even though they had recanted their confessions and insisted they were innocent.

The Insights section is committed to high-quality longform journalism. Our editors work with academics from many different backgrounds who are tackling a wide range of societal and scientific challenges.

Then, in 2009, eight years after Rupp vanished, his car was pulled from a river. His remains were inside, still in one piece, sitting in the driver’s seat. There were no signs that he had been beaten up or cut up. The horrifying story the family had told could not possibly have happened.

The case was reopened, and in a full retrial before the Landshut Regional Court the family was acquitted in 2011. They spent several years in prison for a crime they did not commit, a story they had confessed to under pressure.
No one ever formally investigated how the family’s specific confessions were extracted. The family’s defence had long claimed coercion, and over time some corroborating evidence emerged.

Police had filmed themselves having the suspects “reconstruct” the crime at the farm, and a criminal law professor who later reviewed that footage described the officers’ approach as inquisitorial and leading, saying suspects simply could not be questioned that way.

Separately, a scrap dealer whom police suspected of disposing of Rupp’s car testified at the retrial that, when he would not give the statement investigators wanted, an officer from the same police unit held a service weapon to his head. No officer was investigated. Instead, prosecutors put the scrap dealer on trial for making a false accusation. In December 2012, the court acquitted him.

All four family members were described by their defence lawyer as having cognitive vulnerabilities, which made them especially susceptible to coercive questioning. And although it became clear the family had confessed to something they did not do, they were never compensated, because the retrial court held them partly responsible for their own false statements.
Sadly, the Rupp case is far from unique.
Wrongful convictions and the EUREX database
When Ina Post addressed the audience at the European Innocence Network meeting in Amsterdam in 2019, the room fell silent. Her presence was calm, but the weight of her story was overwhelming.

In 1986, she was wrongfully convicted in the Netherlands of murdering an elderly woman she cared for. The only evidence was a confession. A confession she gave after hours of intense, suggestive police interrogation while in a psychologically vulnerable state. There was no forensic proof, and much of what she had said turned out to be factually incorrect. Still, it took more than two decades of legal struggle before she was finally acquitted in 2010.

Listening to her that day was deeply moving. The room was silent – you could have heard a pin drop. Her story was not just about what had happened to her, it was about how easily justice can go wrong, and how hard it is to make it right again. Her words stayed with us.

As researchers in the field of false confessions and wrongful convictions, we asked ourselves: how many others have suffered similar fates? We knew that the United States tracked exoneration cases through the National Registry of Exonerations, but Europe had no central database, no coordinated effort to track wrongful convictions. There were no numbers, no overview of the problem and no one was trying to change that.

That is why we created EUREX – the European Registry of Exonerations. Its mission is to archive and analyse exonerations across Europe. EUREX is a centralised database that collects and publishes information about cases where individuals were wrongfully convicted and later cleared of all charges.

Beyond documenting these cases, EUREX seeks to understand their causes and consequences, identify systemic patterns, and ultimately contribute to improving legal decision-making. In the long run, we aim to lead empirical research that tests these patterns and informs reforms to prevent future miscarriages of justice.
Wrongful convictions are often thought of as rare and tragic mistakes. But the reality is more complex.
So far, we have documented 150 cases in 20 countries since 1981 in which people were officially declared innocent after years – sometimes decades – behind bars.

Together, these individuals lost more than 970 years of freedom. Our first systematic analysis of the registry (covering the first 144 cases and published in 2026 in Forensic Science International: Synergy) showed that most had been convicted of very serious crimes such as murder or sexual assault. This highlights the devastating consequences when errors occur in high-stakes trials.

These numbers are exactly why a project like EUREX matters: at its launch, Saul Kassin, a social psychologist who specialises in false confessions, described the registry as filling a real gap in the field, one that could give researchers, legal practitioners, and policymakers across Europe a shared evidence base for understanding how wrongful convictions happen – something that has been missing until now.
Innocence lawyer, Geert-Jan Knoops, speaking at the same event, put it more bluntly: “With EUREX, we now have objective proof that we are not dealing with isolated incidents.”
Across the world, false confessions have played a significant role in wrongful convictions. For example, about 35% of the cases in EUREX involve someone who confessed to a crime they did not commit.

Research shows that often false confessions happen to the most vulnerable: teenagers, people with intellectual disabilities, and those with mental health issues. Under pressure in a police interrogation, they may say what the interrogators want to hear – just to get out of the room. In many cases, the combination of personal vulnerabilities and stressful surroundings creates a powerful mix of factors that can lead to a false confession.

Scientists have identified three types of false confessions: voluntary, coerced-compliant and coerced-internalised. A voluntary false confession happens when someone steps forward without any pressure, often to protect someone else, gain attention, or because they mistakenly believe confessing will benefit them. Coerced-compliant confessions occur when a suspect knows they are innocent but gives in simply to end the interrogation or secure what seems like a better deal. Finally, coerced-internalised confessions are the most disturbing: after intense questioning, a person may start doubting their own memory and come to believe they committed the crime.

The kind that shows up most often in courts is the coerced one. These confessions typically follow hours of questioning, psychological manipulation, and physical or emotional exhaustion. Suspects may be deprived of sleep, denied breaks, or led to believe that confessing is the only way out. Without a lawyer present, vulnerable people are especially likely to agree to whatever investigators suggest.

False confession expert Gisli Gudjonsson, writing in a Frontiers in Psychology editorial summarising his own 40-year review of the science, explained: “Until detailed analysis of real-life cases, peer-reviewed research, and DNA exonerations began to emerge in the 1980s and 1990s, it was widely believed that only those with intellectual disabilities or mental illness were susceptible to giving false confessions. This ‘common sense’ view is a fallacy. False confessions are caused by a dynamic process and a combination of ‘risk factors’, which is not confined to the mentally impaired. In fact, most of those who give a coerced confession to police are not mentally impaired.”

Once a confession is made, even if it is false and there is no other evidence, it can shape how everyone sees the case, from law enforcement to judges. It becomes hard to undo. Generally, people assume that no one would confess to something they did not do, so distinguishing false confessions from genuine ones is extremely challenging.
That is why the story of the Rupp family should serve as a warning about what can go wrong when confessions are treated as proof, even when there is no other evidence.
How widespread is the problem?

And yet, these numbers only tell part of the story. EUREX uses a deliberately strict definition: it only includes cases in which someone was convicted by final judgment and later officially cleared after the case was reopened, through an acquittal or a formal declaration of innocence. Countless other cases never clear that bar. Doubts may linger for years, new evidence may surface too late, or legal hurdles, procedural limits and institutional resistance may close the door before a case can be reopened at all. The real number of wrongful convictions is almost certainly higher than any registry can capture.

It is hard to say whether wrongful convictions themselves are becoming more or less frequent. What does seem to be rising is our ability and willingness to catch them. More than half of the exonerations we found happened after 2010, which probably reflects growing efforts to revisit old cases, improve fair investigative practices, and develop more transparent review processes.

One thing the registry makes clear is that wrongful convictions can happen to almost anyone. Exonerees come from different countries, income levels, professions, and ethnic backgrounds. Most are men, but this mirrors the prison population as a whole: men account for the vast majority of people convicted of serious crimes such as murder and sexual assault.
As Saul Kassin, who has spent decades studying wrongful convictions, said in an interview with us:

These are not all the same types of people. This is not about who they are. There are men and women, adults and children, people speaking different languages, from different countries and with different skin colours. Exonerations aren’t limited to a certain type of person – it is a systemic problem.

Wrongful convictions aren’t explained by who the exonerated individuals are, but by what they lose. On average, the exonerees we found were about 36 years old at the time of their conviction – an age when most people are building careers, starting families, and laying plans for the future. Losing those years leaves scars that are personal, social, and financial all at once.

In subsequent interviews, Ina Post has described what that loss feels like: “I was 30 years old when I was arrested. I was married. My husband and I wanted children. While I was in detention, I decided to get a divorce. When you are imprisoned, you rob your partner of their life, too.”

Wrongful convictions are better understood not as a matter of who is convicted, but of how convictions come about. The patterns identified by these cases reflect precisely this: recurring flaws in the processes that produce them.

False confessions, like the ones at the centre of the Rupp and Post cases, appear in 35% of cases we have examined. Flawed forensic evidence played a role in 24%, a reminder that scientific-sounding evidence is only as reliable as the people collecting, evaluating and interpreting it. Eyewitness misidentification (23%) and false accusations (35%) round out the list, underlining just how fallible human memory and perception can be under pressure.

One of the registry’s most striking findings concerns what happens to the actual perpetrator. In 91 cases, an innocent person was convicted for a crime committed by someone else, and in roughly 40% of those, the real culprit was never identified at all.

That means the system failed twice: once by punishing the wrong person, and again by leaving the guilty one free. As Kassin warns: “When you close a case on an innocent person, you leave the offender free to reoffend – and they often do.”

The scale of this risk is stark: a study of 109 real perpetrators later identified in the United States found that 94% went on to commit further crimes, including murder, while innocent people sat behind bars in their place. Failing to catch the true offender does not just deny justice to the wrongfully convicted; it puts the public in danger.
‘My nightmare is over’ – Tomasz Komenda

On New Year’s Eve 1996, 15-year-old Małgorzata Kwiatkowska vanished after a party in Miłoszyce, a small village in south-western Poland. What started as a festive New Year’s Eve ended tragically when her dead body was discovered in the snow the next morning. She had been raped and left to die of internal injuries and hypothermia. The crime scene revealed multiple DNA profiles, bite marks, and other forensic clues – yet for years, the case went cold.

Then, in 2000, a TV programme about the unsolved murder aired a composite sketch of a man seen with Małgorzata on the night she disappeared. A viewer tipped off police, claiming it resembled Tomasz Komenda. Despite thin physical evidence and an alibi that held up, Komenda was arrested, charged, and while insisting he was innocent, convicted in 2003. He was sentenced to 15 years, later extended to 25 years on appeal.

Because Komenda refused to admit guilt, he was ineligible for parole. Over nearly two decades in prison, he endured physical abuse, isolation, and psychological torment, and attempted suicide more than once. “I thought I would never get out,” he later told TVN24. “I thought they would kill me in prison”.

The case cracked open in 2016, when a police officer reviewing old cases spotted major flaws in the original investigation. New DNA testing excluded Komenda entirely and instead pointed to two other men.

Komenda walked free on March 15, 2018, after 18 years in prison. That May, the Polish Supreme Court formally overturned his conviction and declared him innocent. Standing on the courtroom steps after spending 6,540 days behind bars for a crime he did not commit, Komenda told reporters: “My nightmare is over”.

But freedom did not erase what prison had done to him. In a television interview Komenda described how fear and anxiety followed him into daily life. “Even now, I get scared when I hear a loud noise. I still dream about the prison”.

In 2021, he was awarded nearly 13 million zloty (about €2.75 million) in compensation for the years he had lost. But, as he and many other exonerees have said, no amount of money can make up for the lost years.

Psychological research supports what Komenda described. A landmark 2004 study found that wrongfully convicted people often develop post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, and other lasting emotional wounds. In some cases it is severe enough to resemble the aftermath of torture.

A later systematic review reached a similar conclusion, observing that the psychological toll of being wrongfully accused is often severe and long-lasting, and that it can quietly erode someone’s sense of identity, health, relationships, finances, and trust in institutions, while adding a lingering social stigma.

That stigma tends to outlast the conviction itself. Even after exoneration, many people struggle to find work, secure housing, and rebuild a social life. They are often without any of the structured support that is typically offered to parolees. So in practice, being cleared of a crime does not always mean the sentence is over. For many exonerees, it just becomes a different kind of life sentence.

For Komenda, that second sentence was cruelly brief. In May 2024, he died of cancer at just 46 years old. His case prompted a national reckoning in Poland over police misconduct and flawed forensic work, and it pushed the question of how Europe treats exonerees onto the wider public agenda.

Wrongful convictions are not just legal failures. They are human ones. Komenda’s story is a painful reminder of the damage they do and of how long the road to healing can be, even after freedom is won.

Across Europe, reform has often come in the wake of scandal. In the Netherlands, the Schiedammer Park murder case exposed serious flaws in investigative practices and prosecutorial oversight. Public outrage led the College of Procurators General to set up the Commissie-Posthumus in 2005.

Its landmark report identified real vulnerabilities in how criminal cases were built and recommended concrete fixes; among them, bringing in independent forensic advisors and building explicit safeguards against “tunnel vision” – the tendency for investigators to fixate on one suspect and stop questioning their own theory.

These recommendations also led to the creation of the Adviescommissie Afgesloten Strafzaken (ACAS) in 2012, an advisory body that can recommend cases for reopening when new evidence casts doubt on a conviction.

Norway has gone further still, establishing a Criminal Cases Review Commission with full statutory powers to reopen convictions whenever significant new evidence emerges (unlike the Dutch ACAS, which can only advise the Prosecutor General and does not have the power to reopen cases itself).

By December 2020, the Norwegian commission had reopened 351 cases. One of its most striking successes is the case of Viggo Kristiansen, convicted in 2001 (and again on appeal in 2002) of raping and murdering two young girls in Kristiansand, and given Norway’s maximum sentence at the time: 21 years. The case against him rested on a co-defendant’s testimony, weak DNA traces, and a psychological profile. Kristiansen spent nearly two decades insisting he was innocent and filing appeals that went nowhere.

Then in 2021, the commission agreed to reopen the case: new DNA testing excluded him, and witness statements that had previously been dismissed turned out to support his alibi after all. In December 2022, the Borgarting Court of Appeal acquitted him outright, concluding his co-defendant had acted alone. Kristiansen later received substantial compensation. His case makes the argument for independent review bodies: they give a wrongful conviction a real, structured path back to court.

In the United Kingdom, concerns about miscarriages of justice led to the creation of a dedicated review body in 1997 – the Criminal Cases Review Commission. But the watchdog has been plunged into crisis and faced relentless criticism about the way it has handled recent cases.

But such safeguards are far from universal. For example, Belgium and Portugal record zero exonerations in the registry, almost certainly not because their justice systems get it right every time, but because structural barriers make miscarriages of justice harder to surface or overturn in the first place. Narrow rules for reopening closed cases, no independent review commission, and limited legal aid after conviction all add up to a system where mistakes can simply stay buried.

At the European level, the gap is even wider. Criminal justice is still handled almost entirely at the national level, and there’s no EU-wide framework for catching or correcting wrongful convictions. Human rights law offers broad principles, but not the practical tools needed to identify and fix specific errors.
“One does not easily get past 24 lost years,” said Post, who spent four years in prison and more than two decades fighting to finally clear her name.

Wrongful convictions will never be eliminated entirely, but they can be made rarer, easier to detect, and faster to repair. Independent review commissions, safeguards against coercive interrogations, and robust forensic standards are not abstract ideals – they are practical steps grounded in evidence.
Building these reforms into national systems and pooling what is learned across borders is how Europe makes sure that justice does not fail the very people it is meant to protect.

articles.title: Expert reaction: what the Timms review into Pip disability benefits gets right – and where it falls short
articles.author: Stephanie Allen, Research Associate (Mental Health & Wellbeing), University of Glasgow
paras: Personal independence payments (Pip) are welfare benefits that are meant to help people with long-term health issues cope with the extra costs associated with their conditions. But it’s controversial – from the application process to who qualifies.
Sir Stephen Timms, the disability minister, has published a long-awaited report into Pip, recommending a raft of changes to the system.
Here’s what experts made of his findings.
‘Constant dread’ during the application process
Stephanie Allan, Research Associate in Mental Health & Wellbeing, University of Glasgow

Humanising the benefits system, as Timms claims his review will, is crucial. As part of our research, participants told us that applying and being assessed for disability benefits such as Pip has caused psychological distress, particularly for those applying due to conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder or schizophrenia.
We’ve been told assessments can feel like “being on trial”, with constant dread of unexpected letters coming through the door, and can even cause re-traumatisation.

The review’s call to reduce unnecessary reviews and improve communication between assessors and applicants may address these issues – as may its suggestion of training assessors in trauma-informed practice. This means they should offer consistency and transparency in explaining how decisions are made and not minimising people’s difficulties.

Some people living with serious mental health problems face profound challenges and struggle to do things many people take for granted. The report proposes fast-tracked paths for peopel who have “serious, well-evidenced conditions whose impact on their daily life is clear”. But it’s ambiguous which conditions this will cover, and this could also cause worry for potential Pip recipients.

While the Timms review acknowledges the impact of stigma, our work emphasises how negative media reporting and politicians’ speeches about disability benefits can cause distress, especially if it frames claimants as burdens. It can also influence how people respond, and make them even more afraid to participate in society.

People with fluctuating mental health problems have told us that fears of being falsely reported for fraud by neighbours and community members can make them avoid activities such as volunteering, exercise, or even taking part in clinical research that could improve mental health for them or others in future.

Training on trauma-informed care is arguably not enough on its own. Without stronger legal safeguards – such as independent oversight when things go wrong – the power imbalance between claimants and those in charge remains intact.
Furthermore, reforming the claiming process by itself will not make people feel safe if political rhetoric and media narratives continue to frame disabled people as a burden.
Every day is different when you’re disabled
Steve Atkin-Teillet, Lecturer in Law, Nottingham Law School

The nature of some conditions means that symptoms can fluctuate from day to day. The review found that in order to capture the varying nature of a claimant’s needs, the Pip application form should be changed so that it’s simpler for claimants to report what they experience.

This should be underpinned by better training for Pip assessors on the rules surrounding variances and fluctuations in what someone is able to do. This should not only include a requirement to assess whether someone can perform an activity, but also whether they can do so reliably.

Right now, a claimant should only be considered capable of a task if they can do it safely, repeatedly and in a reasonable amount of time. In 2024, I recommended that the new Pip form include these three elements under each activity the claimant describes, as well as on the government’s Pip advice page.

At present, people claiming Pip can be assessed by any type of medical professional. Someone applying for mental health reasons could be given a physiotherapist as their assessor. This is a concern, as claimants sometimes feel their assessor was not competent or well placed to understand their condition.

The Timms review proposes a specific Pip assessor role – but this doesn’t fully address concerns over competency. As it stands, it’s unclear how someone in this new role would be trained to assess a full range of potential disabilities and conditions.
More understanding of neurodiversity since Pip launched
Mindy Ptolomey, Lecturer in Disability Studies, University of Leeds

The review has highlighted that when Pip was designed and implemented – back in 2012 under David Cameron’s coalition government – it did not consider the barriers neurodivergent people face in everyday life. Neither did it take into account their needs in terms of the application process. As pointed out in the interim report of the review, long paper forms with no online version, rigid deadlines, and having to use the phone can all create barriers for neurodivergent people.

The review’s recognition of neurodivergent people’s needs is especially important as the diagnosis of ADHD and autism has increased in recent years. In the UK, new adult autism diagnoses increased more than tenfold from 2010 to 2023, and monthly referrals for ADHD diagnosis more than tripled between 2019 and 2024.

A government review published last month highlights that there is no evidence of widespread over-diagnosis. These increases are instead due to a range of factors like historical under-recognition and greater awareness.

It’s encouraging to see a continued commitment to involving disabled people during the design and implementation stages of any reforms. Disabled people were part of the review’s steering group and their views were included in a range of ways. However, more can be done to make sure the people who face the greatest barriers are included in shaping reforms. Involving neurodivergent people is important for ensuring the core purposes of Pip are delivered supporting disabled people’s independence, participation and autonomy.

Pip can make an important contribution to meeting the additional costs of being disabled, for those in and out of work. The review recommends linking the amount people will receive through Pip more closely to the additional costs they face due to disability or health conditions.

However, questions remain about how these costs will be identified and calculated. Previous data shows that it is difficult for disabled people to understand the additional costs of being disabled, especially when you’ve had a condition all your life, which is the case for neurodivergent people.
Mental health conditions could face cuts
Sarah Ledden, Research Associate in Population Mental Health, King’s College London

One key element of the proposed reforms is to only provide Pip to those who incur additional costs due to a long-term health condition or disability. The challenge here will be creating appropriate mechanisms to assess these costs, without repeating current difficulties the system has in evaluating fluctuating and ‘harder-to-see’ conditions.

The Department for Work and Pensions recently released a research report which aimed to understand the disability-related needs that create additional living costs among Pip recipients. It indicated that people with mental health conditions were less likely to have additional costs for equipment and travel needs, though they did more often have paid treatment needs (such as counselling).

However, these people experience employment and income gaps, earning 32% less than people with no such conditions, and higher levels of financial hardship. This indicates that there are often financial challenges for people with mental health conditions, but many of these costs may be hidden or cumulative.

If the transition to a new benefit is managed poorly, with proposed impact assessments not designed to capture these types of costs, it risks people with mental health conditions being left behind. The Timms review has recommendations around understanding inequalities in experiences and outcomes of different groups, which will be vital in ensuring the system works.

The DWP’s evidence published with the review reported that only 1 in 5 Pip claimants reported having a single condition. Most people reported multiple conditions. Only 4.4% of total Pip claims are those solely claiming for depression and anxiety, with these more often reported alongside other conditions.
The rise in these cases is based on the “primary condition” reported on Pip claims, although this is in line with evidence that these conditions are rising in the general population.

Previous research from our team on Pip receipt among people who accessed specialist mental healthcare found that receiving Pip is related to greater clinical need (including diagnosis type and longer time receiving care). If the government aims to reduce welfare spending by assessing mental health Pip claims using stricter criteria, this may not have as big an impact as they expect.
This article was corrected on November 27 to remove a reference to Pip being a UK-wide benefit. In Scotland it was replaced with adult disability payment in 2025.

articles.title: Russell Brand and the ‘blokeification’ of Christianity
articles.author: Jonathan Abernethy-Barkley, Lecturer in Theology and Religious Studies, King's College London
paras: When Russell Brand was sentenced to ten years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault in November 2026, a peculiar image stood out: his rosary.
Various news outlets reported that Brand was using a rosary during his sentencing. Reporters even caught sight of a crucifix through the window of the prison van that transported him.

As both a sociologist of religion and an ordained minister, I am not necessarily preoccupied with whether Brand is a sincere Christian. Instead, I am interested in what this public display of faith says about the shifting links between religion, masculinity and celebrity culture. This has led me to look into what I call the “blokeification” of Christianity. Something that will be explored further in my forthcoming book, Global Awakenings Populism, Conspirituality & Conversion Narratives.

In a British context, I would describe the “blokeification” of Christianity as an attempt to reshape Christian faith and religious identity through a masculine, often laddish, lens. It’s a move that pushes back against the idea that church is excessively formal, sentimental, or feminine.

In recent years, I have seen this in churches where religious belief is discussed over a pint in a pub, where football and “banter” build community, and where leaders try to present themselves as ordinary, relatable blokes. There is nothing inherently wrong with making church more relatable for men, but it is worth questioning the particular kind of masculinity it projects.

This is especially obvious in certain online Christian circles where faith starts to merge with gym culture, self-improvement and established gender roles. While many churches and religious groups are working to push back against the kind of masculinity promoted by personalities such as Andrew Tate, is equally important to examine how Christianity itself might be building and promoting its own specific masculine ideals.

At the same time, even if they aren’t coming from the same religious groups, more populist and far-right movements are appropriating Christian symbols. In these spaces, Christianity becomes less about actual belief or practice and more about cultural identity, nationalism and masculine strength.
Muscular Christianity and blokeification

In the UK, you could argue that the roots of this go back to the muscular Christianity movement of the mid-Victorian era. Starting in the 1850s, several clergymen and educators felt that Christianity had become too passive, domestic and disconnected from men’s lives.

Through writers like Charles Kingsley and Thomas Hughes, they pushed to reclaim – or “blokeify” – Christianity by focusing on physical strength and moral character. This played out in the growing connection between Christianity and organised sports. In fact, many of Britain’s most famous football clubs (including Manchester City, Aston Villa and Bolton Wanderers) started as church teams in the late 1800s.

Similar ideals can be found in the Boys Brigade, which combined religious teaching with military-style drills, and in the Young Men’s Christan Association (the YMCA), founded in London in 1844, which combined physical strength, moral worldview formation and shared community experiences.

The core strategy of such movements hasn’t changed much: take the secular spaces where men already hang out and fill them with Christian meaning. While the Victorians used rugby pitches and boxing rings to show that a man could be both tough and devout, modern blokeified Christianity uses pubs, five-a-side football, gyms and podcasts to do the same thing.
This brings us back to Russell Brand and how he fits within these wider sociological trends in religion.

The public presentation of Brand’s coming to faith appeared less concerned with a Damascene encounter (a sudden and transformative religious experience, akin to St Paul’s conversion on the road to Damascus), and more with a rugged, performative expression of Christianity, laden with celebrity culture. Brand’s media-friendly baptism in the River Thames, stripped to the waist and wearing swimming shorts, was presided over not by an ordained minister but by celebrity adventurer Bear Grylls. Brand would later replicate the ritual for another convert, this time wearing water-drenched white briefs.
Responding to the backlash, Brand remarked: “It might seem a bit soon to be baptising people, but the Apostles did it on day one, so here we are.”

In aligning his expressions of faith with the manosphere, Brand followed an increasingly well-trodden path among influencers and conspiracy theorists, drawing on Christian rhetoric to legitimise and market their particular interpretations of the world.
Then, there is the question of style over substance. Brand was pictured carrying a Bible to court, and even released a step-by-step guide to becoming a Christian in seven days.

But his apparent difficulty recalling or accurately quoting scripture during interviews raises questions about the relationship between the public performance of Christianity and the slower, less glamorous process of religious formation.

While Brand’s flashier moments of conversion have dominated the headlines, the quieter work of faith – and the real test of character – usually plays out away from the spotlight. Seen through that lens, Brand’s public turn to religion is less a standalone curiosity than a mirror of how masculinity and celebrity culture are reshaping faith today.

articles.title: Andy Burnham’s Brussels deal throws up a paradox for both sides in the EU debate
articles.author: Benjamin Martill, Senior Lecturer in Politics and International Relations, University of Edinburgh
paras: At a summit in Brussels this month, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham revealed breakthroughs in the UK-EU “reset” begun under his predecessor Keir Starmer.

The summit produced agreement on several important issues. New rules from March 2028 will remove the need for certification of animal and food products, UK and EU emissions trading systems (ETS) will be linked, and a youth experience scheme will enable up to 100,000 18 to 31-year-olds to work and study in the UK or EU.
And in the meantime, both sides reaffirmed their commitment to working towards a closer relationship.

Yet the announcement came in for criticism from the political right. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued that Burnham had “oversold” the deal when he presented it to parliament. She said the prime minister was trying to take Britain “back to 2015”.
Meanwhile, Reform UK’s leader Nigel Farage claimed the agreement amounted to a betrayal of Brexit.
A lightning rod for criticism

Notably, the reset appears to be garnering more intense criticism than it did under Starmer. One reason for this is that the stakes are now higher. Burnham has already sought to shift the dial on Europe and has openly flirted with the possibility of the UK rejoining the EU.
Both sides see the summit an opportunity to lay the groundwork for the bigger fight to come.

Criticism of the deal is already having a chilling effect. Burnham has been noticeably more coy in his language about rejoining the EU, insisting in his remarks to the House of Commons that he would seek to rejoin only if it was in the UK’s interests – and on the back of a new referendum.
But the criticism from the Conservatives and Reform of the reset announcement misses the point. What it actually does is highlight the limitations of being outside the EU.

Badenoch’s claim that Burnham oversold the deal partly reflects the numbers involved, which look small but are in fact significant. The promised 0.4% increase in GDP amounts to a significant economic boost at a time when UK growth has been sluggish. This is hardly trivial.

Meanwhile, the non-EU trade deals preferred by Reform and the Conservatives have resulted in a far smaller contributon to UK growth than Burnham’s reset deal. UK accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), for instance, is associated with an anticipated boost to GDP just one tenth the size of the current reset.
And yes, Badenoch may be right that the figure is not going to change the world. But this reflects the limitations imposed by Brexit more than anything else.

Back in 2016, the Leave campaign claimed that withdrawing from the EU would not disproportionately affect the trading relationship with the bloc. That turned out to be illusory, as the EU correctly surmised that affording the UK special treatment would undermine the value of membership and lead to the disintegration of the internal market.

Thus, the EU has opposed efforts by the UK to negotiate piecemeal integration into the single market – which it describes as “cherry picking”. Perhaps unsurprisingly, it has only been willing to negotiate on specific areas where it sees a discernible benefit for the bloc.

The real limitation of Burnham’s deal is not a lack of ambition, but the strictures imposed by Brexit. And getting that 0.4% figure up would mean being open to more radical forms of re-engagement – as Burnham is indeed doing. (Estimates of the economic benefits of rejoining the EU are between 4%-6% of GDP).

Badenoch also notes, correctly, that the deal requires the UK to align with EU rules. But again, this is a symptom of Brexit, which removed the UK from EU decision-making forums and from any say over these rules. Since Brexit, the UK has continued to mimic EU rules in many areas – including state aid – without having any influence over them.

Solving the UK’s rule-taker problem arguably points to the benefits of rejoining. This would return the UK’s place within the EU’s legislative process and solve the so-called “democratic deficit” afflicting third-party countries participating in the internal market.

The simultaneous conversations on the reset and rejoining the EU result in a paradox for both sides. For the right, criticising Burnham’s agreement offers a means of heading off further moves towards the EU. But it also highlights the very real limitations of what is possible outside that framework.
And for Burnham and Labour europhiles, the need to tout the agreement as a success misses a clear opportunity to highlight the limits of Brexit and the benefits of rejoining.
Both sides, in their own way, miss what the reset really makes clear. That is that the deal exposes the continued trade-offs of Brexit and the limits of what is possible outside the EU.
Hence the political right may inadvertently bolster the case for rejoining – while Labour proudly showcases what can be achieved from the outside.

Benjamin Martill is affiliated with Chatham House and the Independent Commission on UK-EU Relations and has previously received funding from the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme.

articles.title: Accurate job descriptions and pay transparency shouldn’t be radical ideas
articles.author: Julia Yates, Professor of Organisational Psychology, City St George's, University of London
paras: Salary negotiations can feel like a bit of a game, but new UK legislation may change the rules. Under draft government plans, employers will be required to publish the salary range for any job advertised.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised a legal requirement for pay transparency in job adverts. There have also been proposals for equal pay reforms for those with disabilities or of an ethnic minority.
However, the Equality and Human Rights Commission is going further. It is urging governments to prevent employers from asking candidates about their existing salaries or expectations.

Recruitment is a game played on a very uneven playing field. Hiring the wrong recruit can be expensive and time consuming. But the toll placed on someone who finds themselves in the wrong job can be deep and enduring, potentially damaging their physical and mental health, work engagement, job satisfaction, and diminishing their confidence in their own abilities.

Employers have traditionally used previous earnings as a benchmark or indication of the salary a candidate would be prepared to accept. It’s also a proxy for their value – assuming that we are all worth what other people have decided to pay us.

From a potential employer’s perspective, a candidate’s high previous salary is understood as a sign of “latent quality”. This means it’s an indication of hidden abilities and skills that might not have been revealed at the interview.

Candidates can, of course, refuse to disclose their salary, but even that comes at a cost. It could give the impression that they are less skilled and have fewer alternative options. Gender stereotypes lead recruiters to believe that men are more comfortable discussing money, so they are viewed with more suspicion if reluctant to disclose their current earnings.

Questions about salary expectations can also be tricky for candidates to manage. Opt too low and you risk being offered a lower starting salary. Too high and you reduce your chances of a job offer. Evidence suggests that a collaborative approach and a precise starting bid seem to serve candidates well in their salary negotiations. For example, asking for £34,575 works better than £35,000.
Making salaries fairer for all

Much of the gender pay gap can be traced back to starting salaries. The explanations for this are complex, but include the anchoring effects of the salaries that recruiters expect to pay. This includes lower initial rates for female candidates, and the salaries that candidates feel able to ask for: men are more likely to negotiate hard when it comes to their starting salary, and employers are more likely to concede to their demands.

A similar story is seen with ethnicity. Certain groups – for example Black candidates and those from south-east and east Asia – seem to come out of negotiations with a worse deal. Racial and gender stereotypes can influence both candidates’ and recruiters’ behaviour.

The current system of anchoring future salaries to previous salaries perpetuates discrimination, allowing people who hold privilege to cling on to an early advantage throughout their careers. Differences in starting salaries endure for years and it’s estimated that two thirds of the steady-state gender pay gap in the UK – meaning the wage gap that would occur if employment levels were constant and steady, rather than fluctuating as they do now – can be traced back to gender differences in starting salaries.

Furthermore, job adverts are not always an accurate reflection of what the role entails. They’re designed to sell the job to prospective employees. AI-curated job adverts are beginning to sound similar, making it ever harder for a candidate to work out whether they would actually like the job.
Typical AI-generated job adverts are often vague and are full of corporate buzzwords, leaving the potential candidate unsure about what the employer is looking for.

Job descriptions often reflect an idealised account of the role. They are generally written from the perspective of the employer rather than employee. For this reason, they can be light on the day-to-day realities.

Employers might offer interview candidates the chance to ask questions, but this is generally just an extension of the selection process. All parties are aware that this is not the time for an honest conversation.

Experiences vary, but candidates often have little more than a job advert and a single interview to go on. Ultimately this may well backfire for the employer. The organisation might find themselves with the “best” candidate on paper. But if they have missold the job, or misrepresented the organisation, it can lead to unrealistically high employee expectations, lower job satisfaction and a higher chance that their new recruit will quit their job.

“Realistic job previews”, where employers give an honest account of what the job is actually like, have been shown to have a positive impact on employers’ ability to recruit and retain good candidates. Studies have shown that when employees are invited to talk to candidates honestly about the job and the organisation, and are open about the challenges and stresses, potential recruits feel more positive about the integrity of the employer. Their expectations of the role are also more realistic, and they end up performing better and wanting to stay with the new organisation.

Staff turnover is an expensive business. Annual employee turnover across the UK is 34% on average. The cost of replacing each employee earning £25,000 or more is approximately £30,614 for the employer. Any improvements that can be made to the selection process to ensure that new hires are in it for the long haul could reap significant financial rewards.

The plans to increase transparency in salary negotiations feel like a step in the right direction, but providing an accurate description of the job shouldn’t be hailed as a radical approach. Job selection is the start of an ongoing relationship which is bound to be more successful if it starts with more transparency and collaboration.

articles.title: If politicians really want to cut heating bills they need to trust in green energy – businesses already are
articles.author: Renaud Foucart, Senior Lecturer in Economics, Lancaster University Management School, Lancaster University
paras: This year’s United Nations climate summit, Cop31, ended in Antalya without a deal.
It appears that the world’s politicians and policy makers have collectively moved on from building a global coalition against climate change, just as its effects are becoming impossible to ignore.
Yet the public have not stopped worrying. In a 2025 global Ipsos survey, 64% of adults said failing to act on climate change would hurt future generations.
And in 2026 around 60% of American adults think global efforts will not be enough to avoid the worst effects of climate change.

But perhaps the biggest hurdle to making more climate-friendly changes is the current cost-of-living crisis. It appears to be politically difficult to tell cash-strapped voters to be more environmentally friendly.

Opponents of policies tackling climate change, including British and European right-wing parties and Donald Trump, seem to have effectively persuaded a majority of the public that it is impossible to make climate-friendly choices and keep your bills down. In 2026, 62% of the UK public expected net zero – Britain’s route to climate neutrality – to increase their bills in the short run.
Voters often tend to overestimate how much they would lose from a carbon tax, and to underestimate how much others care.
But despite this, people are starting to notice that climate action cannot be blamed for an economic and environmental crisis fuelled by gas and petrol prices.
The 62% share of voters who think net zero increases their bills is the lowest on record. And 51% expect net zero to be good for the economy in the long run – only 24% think it will hurt it.

Politicians are right to be careful about what voters will accept. French president Emmanuel Macron has learned the hard way, after ten years of public protests, that taxing petrol is unpopular. In Milan, some voters owning polluting cars said they were likely to vote for the far right when the city banned their vehicles from the city centre.
But very few politicians make the point that the cost-of-living crisis would be much worse without green policy.
Cost-of-living crisis is a fossil fuel crisis
In 2021, Russia supplied around 40% of the EU’s pipeline gas imports. Scrambling to replace these imports with liquefied gas from Qatar and the US has sent energy prices through the roof.

Because of its past dependency on Russian fossil fuels, Europe now pays around ten times more than the US for the same quantity of gas. These high prices have hurt the economy and pushed up inflation.
Every unit of electricity generated by wind turbines, solar panels and nuclear power plants cuts consumer bills.

Those resources saved £5.9 billion in gas imports for the UK at the start of the Iran conflict when shipping was blocked through the Strait of Hormuz. Every time no gas is needed to produce electricity, prices come down.

Significant economic damage can be caused by ignoring this. It has been clear for some time now that the future is made of electric cars and batteries. Yet European carmakers still lobby for a perpetual delay of the transition.
This strategy is costing jobs today, having transformed Europe’s leading carmakers into global laggards.
And it also hurts consumers. The world’s cheapest electric cars are made in China. EU efforts to protect what remains of its car industry using tariffs mean they cost consumers 45% more.
Britain has so far avoided the extra cost. But the EU is pushing it to impose similar tariffs.
Business is investing in green energy

But global investors are not as backward-looking as governments. This year, green energy investment is expected to reach US$2.2 trillion (£1.68 trillion) – almost double the investment in fossil fuels, and double the global investment in artificial intelligence. More than 90% of large-scale renewable investment in 2025 was cheaper than the cheapest fossil fuel alternative.
The same self-interested approach could apply to ordinary citizens.
An electric car costs less to run than a petrol one. But delays in the transition mean there are still too few charging points to make it practical for everyone.

Another factor is that in England, for instance, road congestion is taking an increasing toll on the economy, and this primarily affects motorists. Even in the US, where public transport accounts for less than 1% of journeys, when subways are not working, these few passengers switching to the car increase road congestion by 47%.
Pro-car lobbies do try to block investment in walkable cities and public transport. Will they take responsibility for the projected 85% increase in British road congestion by 2040?

Migration is very high on voters’ list of concerns, higher than any other in some British polls. And the consequences of climate change, such as flooding and high temperatures, are among the top reasons people leave their home countries. Without international cooperation on issues like water and energy, the flow of people wanting to escape poverty to live in less affected countries is likely to go up.
We live in an ageing world, and it appears that people are increasingly scared of change. The global mood feels protectionist and as crises accumulate, many want to put their own country first.
Very few environmental activists or politicians seem to speak to these instincts.

But green electricity makes you independent from foreign dictators, global cooperation should make migration more manageable, and many of our current problems come from ignoring climate change, not from trying to address it.

articles.title: The Hillsborough Law requires public servants to be honest – but what does honesty actually mean?
articles.author: Byron Hyde, Philosopher of Science and Public Policy, Hokkaido University; Bangor University; University of Bristol
paras: The Hillsborough disaster in 1989 ultimately claimed the lives of 97 Liverpool fans. In the weeks that followed, South Yorkshire Police reviewed its officers’ written accounts before passing them to the official inquiry.

The Hillsborough Independent Panel later found that 164 statements had been substantially changed. In 116 of them, comments critical of the force were removed or altered. In 2021, two former officers and the force’s solicitor were tried over those changes. The case collapsed. The judge ruled that the original inquiry wasn’t a statutory one, and the police had no legal duty of candour there.

The public office (accountability) bill, known as the Hillsborough law, currently in the House of Lords, is meant to close that gap. Covering up to 1.9 million public servants, it would require authorities and officials to act with “candour, transparency and frankness” towards inquiries and investigations. Breaching that duty with the aim of obstructing them would be a crime. The bill also creates a new offence of misleading the public, with a maximum sentence of two years in prison.

Honesty has been one of the seven principles of public life since 1995. Hillsborough shows what can happen when a moral duty may be ignored at little cost. But once honesty becomes a legal duty, someone has to decide what it requires. That’s much harder than it sounds.
Honesty is more than not lying

Research on public health communication shows that official messages can fall short of honesty without anyone telling a lie. They might use true statements to create a false impression, which is known as paltering. For example, they can leave out the size of a benefit or the harms, strip out uncertainty, or present risks in whatever form looks most persuasive.

Imagine a council official is asked at an inquiry whether they were warned that a block of flats was unsafe. They reply: “I never received a report saying the building was unsafe.” That may be strictly true. But suppose they had received several emails from residents and a fire officer raising concerns about the building’s fire doors. Nothing they said was false, yet the inquiry would come away with the wrong picture.
The Hillsborough statements fit the same pattern: the deception lay in what had been taken out.

The bill seems to accept this. Its test for “seriously improper” conduct refers to dishonesty “whether by means of falsehood, concealment, obfuscation or otherwise”. It says an “act” includes “an omission or a course of conduct”. And the duty of candour requires officials to correct “any errors or omissions” in what they have already told an inquiry.
But the bill uses the word “dishonesty” without defining it. Nor does it say what counts as “misleading”. That’s important because the line is blurry.

Every statement leaves something out. The duty of candour asks officials to provide information that’s “relevant to the inquiry or investigation”, but someone still has to decide what’s relevant. Not every omission is a cover-up.

The problem grows when the evidence is incomplete or disputed. To show that someone misled others, a court needs something to compare their statement with. Should that be the truth as it later emerged, or the best understanding at the time? Early in a public health emergency, for example, officials often have to speak before the science is settled.

This is why the difference between misinformation and disinformation matters. Misinformation is false or misleading content shared without meaning to deceive, whereas disinformation is spread on purpose. An official may give an inaccurate account because they were wrongly briefed, or may not have realised a detail mattered. That’s a failure, but not necessarily dishonesty.
Can honesty really be enforced through the law?

The bill deals with this through what lawyers call the “mental element” of an offence. To be guilty of misleading the public, officials must “act with the intention of misleading the public” or be “reckless as to whether their act will do so”. They must also “know, or ought to know, that their act is seriously improper”.

An act is only seriously improper if it “involved dishonesty that was significant or repeated” on a matter of significant public concern, caused or risked harm, and departed significantly from proper conduct.

This leaves courts with a hard task. Proving intent means piecing together what an official knew and believed at the time. Omissions are especially hard to prove. A prosecutor must show that the official had the information, understood that it mattered and chose not to share it.

Draw these boundaries too narrowly and the selective editing seen after Hillsborough could slip through again, because every sentence left in was technically true. Draw them too vaguely and officials may say less, hedge everything and send every statement through lawyers.
Criminal law also has to be clear enough for people to know in advance what’s forbidden. Honesty is a tricky concept, so it’s likely the Hillsborough law will be difficult to enforce.

The Hillsborough law already accepts that dishonesty can mean “concealment” or “obfuscation”, not just “falsehood”. What it doesn’t yet do is say where honest selection ends and dishonest concealment begins. Peers still have a chance to fix this by defining “dishonesty” and “misleading” in the bill or its guidance.

For public servants bound by the law, there is a practical lesson. “Did I say anything false?” is the wrong question. A better one is: “Will the people I’m speaking to come away with an accurate picture?”
Byron Hyde previously received funding from the Wellcome Trust to investigate the seven principles of public life.

articles.title: Solving the Neet crisis may come with a price tag the government can’t afford
articles.author: Peter Urwin, Director, Centre for Employment Research, University of Westminster
paras: The UK’s one million 16 to 24-year-olds who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) are again at the centre of political and media debate, thanks to Alan Milburn’s latest review. The review’s diagnosis is correct: the challenge is not only young people’s skills and readiness for work, but also a shortage of jobs for them. So will the proposals solve the crisis?

Milburn – a former Labour minister – essentially suggests a fresh take on Labour’s New Deal for Young People (NDYP) from the 1990s. This mandated that people aged 18 to 24 who were long-term unemployed had to take up options to get them back into work. These options included a subsidised job, full-time education or training. If they did not participate, they faced benefit sanctions.

Back then, there was also a period of support. Taken together, these resemble the guarantee proposed in Milburn’s report. This has a period of early support; a menu of options (college, training, apprenticeship, work placement, civic service and help to start a business). There is also a paid job as part of the jobs guarantee, as well as an expectation that young people engage with the support.
Some of our earliest research focused on the NDYP, and we have continued to evaluate how the programme and the training provided improved employment prospects for young people.
So does evidence support the review’s suggestion that reforms will help an additional 440,000 young people into work by 2036? Unfortunately not.

It is true that by October 2001, more than three years after it started, 244,000 young people had left NDYP for sustained and unsubsidised jobs. But a large number would have found work anyway and the additional contribution of NDYP in its first two years was estimated at between 8,000 and 20,000.

A comparison from think tank the Resolution Foundation of costs per job suggests Milburn’s reforms need to be about three times as effective as previous employment schemes. Given the New Deal’s modest net effects, the gap may be wider still.
What’s more, nearly half (44%) of young people who are Neet are not claiming out-of-work benefits, so any expectation to engage, backed by the potential for benefit sanctions, will have less weight.
Whole-system change is unlikely

Milburn is correct to say that tackling the UK’s longstanding Neet challenge requires change across the “whole system”. But achieving that requires substantial funding. As such, the review is pitched to secure this money against competition from social care, housing, defence and the criminal justice system. Milburn projects a substantial return on investment, but as with any review, he is making the case to the Treasury.

It is a risky strategy to go for whole-system change in a world where so many other policy areas demand the same. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has accepted Milburn’s core principles, but stopped short of committing to all its recommendations. Any new money will be dependent on a white paper in the new year and the 2027 Spending Review, where it will compete with many other pressures.

The review has a package of hiring incentives worth around £1.1 billion a year at its peak. But it is counting on these subsidies to do most of the work of creating opportunities at a time of crisis in entry-level jobs.

Milburn proposes that further education and apprenticeship expansion should have “first call” on substantial new investment. We strongly agree, but this needs to go much further. Further education is best placed to link the whole system, but long-term deterioration in the sector’s financial position is likely to continue without substantial additional support.

Colleges are where many of the young people at risk of becoming Neet find their path from age 16. Schools are funded for pupils before the age they may become Neet. Colleges are funded only if they enrol a young person and keep them learning – stopping them becoming Neet. Colleges have stronger incentives to seek out those at risk, but must be funded to provide an experience that re-engages young people.

One way round the shortage of jobs is to train more young people for work where employers already cannot find enough staff – electricians, carpenters and bricklayers, for example, as well as engineers and technicians. The commitment to apprenticeships is encouraging, but other promises in this area have not been met.

When it comes to AI, some takeaways from the latest research are that office jobs in routine professions (such as legal services, market research, trading and finance operations) are most exposed, while construction, installation, maintenance, repair and skilled trades are less exposed. Further education is where these skills are built.

Technology is also lowering the cost of experimenting with self-employment. The Milburn report drew on our work for the Youth Futures Foundation (an organisation to help marginalised young people to find work) and highlighted it as a route for young people who need flexibility because of health, disability or caring responsibilities. The offer – up to £500 to explore an idea, a £3,000 grant and “specialist support” – is welcome, but the review does not say what that support is, nor who judges which ideas are viable.

The ambition of Alan Milburn’s report is much needed, but the whole-system change it proposes is unlikely to be funded. It is vital to be imaginative in taking forward aspects of the review that embrace the risks and disruptions that are coming to the labour market. That means putting further education at the centre, building the skills that AI struggles to replace, backing self-employment and evaluating the reforms rigorously as they roll out.
Peter Urwin has received funding from the Economic and Social Research Council and the Nuffield Foundation to research the experiences of young people at risk of Neet.

articles.title: Companies are getting less accurate data on extreme weather just when they need it the most
articles.author: Suvrat Dhanorkar, Associate Professor of Operations Management, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples.

But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather.

To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027.
That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in.

But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting, which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses.

As a scholar of business operations and sustainability, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices.
Gaps in climate science grow

In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts. The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars.

This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record.

While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024.

For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity. Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data.
Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening.

In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline, while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites, which feed forecast models.

Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit, while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database.
What this means for supply chains

The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling.

In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains.

Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models.

When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services.

While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t.
And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin.
What it means for consumers

Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves.
Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year.
And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026.
A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth.
