articles.title: The stunning transformation of the Southern Democratic Party, in one lifetime
articles.author: Gibbs Knotts, Professor of Political Science, Coastal Carolina University
paras: Two of the biggest surprises of the 2026 election cycle were Democratic U.S. Senate victories in the Deep South. In addition to Annie Andrews’ victory in South Carolina, Scott Colom won a close contest in Mississippi, a place that historian James Cobb called “The Most Southern Place on Earth.”

Colom is not Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator. Two Black Republicans represented the state during Reconstruction, when state legislatures still selected U.S. senators. But Colom is the state’s first popularly elected Black U.S. senator. He is also the first Democrat that Mississippians have sent to the Senate since 1982.

It is tempting to read this change using a familiar political science term: party realignment. But as political scientists who study political campaigns and Southern politics, we see an equally important transformation in the electorate – the people who can cast votes.

Simply put, the Democratic Party in the South was transformed from a party that defended white supremacy and Black disenfranchisement into one in which Black voters became a central constituency. The Democrats who held Mississippi’s Senate seats for the majority of the 20th century were chosen by an electorate built to exclude Black citizens. Colom was elected by a dramatically different electorate and represents a very different Democratic Party.
To understand the magnitude of the change in Mississippi, it helps to look at the Democrats who came before Colom, what they stood for, and the political power they wielded.
Reconstruction and its end

For a brief period after the Civil War, Black Mississippians exercised real political power. They were a majority of the state’s population and, with the right to vote, helped elect the state Legislature that sent Hiram Revels to the U.S. Senate in 1870 and Blanche Bruce in 1875, both of them Black.

That period did not last. White Democrats regained control of Mississippi government in the 1870s, aided by political violence, intimidation and electoral fraud. In 1890, the state adopted a new constitution that used poll taxes, literacy tests and other restrictions to systematically disfranchise Black voters. Two years after the new constitution took effect, the percentage of Black men registered to vote had fallen to just 5.4 percent.

The result fundamentally changed Mississippi politics. For the next several generations, the Democratic Party dominated a political system in which most Black Mississippians had little meaningful voice. Republican electoral victories were rare. One newspaper in 1963 claimed that the election of Lewis McAllister to the state House was the party’s first win in 43 years. Without a competitive general election, winning the Democratic primary often meant winning office, and the politicians who emerged from a one-party system made possible by Black disenfranchisement became some of the most powerful political figures in the state’s history.

What happened in Mississippi reflected a broader pattern across the South. In 1949, political scientist V.O. Key published his seminal study of the region, “Southern Politics in State and Nation.” Key argued that the solid Democratic South rested on systematic disenfranchisement of Black voters.

The one-party system helped keep Black Southerners out of political power while allowing white Southern politicians to present a unified front against efforts to dismantle segregation and expand Black voting rights, particularly when those efforts came from the federal government. Mississippi was among the clearest examples of that system.
Segregation and political power

Before Colom, the last Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi was John Stennis in 1982. He first won election in 1947, filling the seat of Theodore Bilbo, who had won reelection in 1946 after a campaign in which he urged white Mississippians to keep Black voters away from the polls. Stennis won a 1947 special election with 52,068 votes in a state of 2.2 million people. He held that seat for 41 years.

Throughout much of his career, Stennis was an ardent segregationist. In 1956, he was one of 101 members of Congress from the South who signed what was called the “Southern Manifesto.” In that statement, these lawmakers denounced the Supreme Court’s decision in Brown v. Board of Education, in which the justices ruled that the “separate but equal” standards of racial segregation were unconstitutional; Stennis and the other signatories pledged resistance to school desegregation.
Later in his Senate career, Stennis was the only Southern Democrat who voted to oppose the creation of a national holiday honoring Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.

Stennis’ Senate colleague for much of his tenure, Mississippi Democrat James Eastland, was an equally staunch defender of segregation. A cotton planter from the Mississippi Delta, he was appointed to the Senate in 1941 and won the seat outright in 1942. He remained in the Senate until 1978.

The day after the Supreme Court handed down its 1954 decision in Brown v. Board of Education, Eastland was quoted saying, “the South will not abide by nor obey this legislative decision by a political court.”

Recent attention has understandably focused on Stennis, the last Democrat to represent Mississippi in the Senate. When Colom takes office, he will occupy the Senate seat once held by Eastland and Democrat James Vardaman, who said that “if it is necessary every Negro in the state will be lynched; it will be done to maintain white supremacy.”

One-party rule also gave Mississippi’s senators unusual power. With little electoral competition, they could remain in office for decades. In a Senate where seniority mattered, longevity translated into influence.

Eastland, for example, chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee for more than two decades, giving him enormous influence over civil rights legislation. During his chairmanship of the powerful committee, that committee became known as “the graveyard of civil rights legislation,” according to the Senate’s website.

The Voting Rights Act of 1965 helped dismantle the electoral system that had sustained these men in office. Before it, fewer than 10% of Black Mississippians were even registered to vote. Within a few short years, a majority were.

Black voters increasingly aligned with the Democratic Party as its national leaders embraced civil rights, even while many Democratic officeholders in Mississippi continued to defend segregation. That meant Black voters sometimes supported incumbent white segregationists. The party’s voters changed faster than many of its candidates did.

The 1978 election for the seat Colom will hold illustrates how complicated that transition could be. After Eastland retired, Charles Evers, brother of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, ran as an independent and drew nearly a quarter of the vote. His candidacy split the traditionally Democratic vote, helping Republican Thad Cochran win with a mere plurality.
By the 21st century, white Mississippians overwhelmingly supported Republican candidates, and Republican dominance had replaced the old Democratic dominance in most statewide elections.
That pattern made Colom’s victory all the more striking. He won with overwhelming support from Black voters while also attracting enough white voters to build a winning statewide coalition.

The contrast with Mississippi’s old Democratic coalition could hardly be sharper. The Democratic Party of Vardaman, Bilbo, Eastland and Stennis maintained its power in part by keeping Black Mississippians away from the ballot box with violence and Jim Crow laws.
When Colom is sworn in, Revels’ old seat will, for the first time, be held by a Black senator directly elected by Mississippi voters.

articles.title: A Westmoreland County easement shows how landowners can protect farmland without selling it
articles.author: Andrew P. Morriss, Professor of Law, Bush School & School of Law, Texas A&M University; Institute for Humane Studies
paras: Scott Tomlinson still owns the 35 acres in Ligonier Township in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, that his family has cared for over seven generations. But in July 2026, he sold part of what it means to own them.

For US$139,000, Tomlinson gave the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy the right to enforce restrictions on how the land is used, TribLive reported. The restrictions protect its farmland and woods from future development in perpetuity.

According to the report, the property is about 80% forest, with slopes that drain into a tributary of Loyalhanna Creek. It includes habitat for buffalo nut, a shrub the state lists as a rare species of concern, and farm soils the USDA classifies as “farmland of statewide importance.”
That is how a conservation easement works: The land stays privately owned, but its owners agree to limits on what they can do with it.
Such agreements let today’s landowners make conservation decisions that bind future owners.

In more than two decades of studying private land conservation, I have found that deciding which rights to give up, how to pay for conservation and how to handle future changes can be complicated. My family has also spent roughly two years negotiating an easement on our own family’s ranch in Texas.
Dividing the rights of ownership

Think of land ownership as a bundle of sticks, with each stick representing a different property right. Within the limits of the law, owners can build on the land, farm it, subdivide it and more. An easement separates particular rights from the rest of the bundle.

For example, an access easement gives someone else the right to cross your property. In a conservation easement, the landowner voluntarily gives up the right to use the land in specified ways. A land trust or government agency receives the right to enforce those limits.

Imagine someone who owns a 1,000-acre farm that has long been in her family. Development is spreading into the surrounding countryside, and neighboring farms are being divided into smaller properties or subdivisions. She wants her land to stay largely intact. One stick in her bundle is the right to subdivide.

A farmer who grants an easement might agree to limit how many parcels future owners can carve out of the farm while still allowing farming. The farmer could still sell the property or pass it on, but whoever owns it next would also be bound by the restrictions, because the farmer can’t sell rights the farmer no longer owns. Those future owners may have no intention of subdividing. But the farmer who signs the easement can’t know what their children, or someone who buys the farm a century from now, will want to do.

Tomlinson’s worry – that land his family has cared for since the 1870s could be sold off for development once he’s gone – plays out against a broader shift in the county’s farm landscape. According to the USDA Census of Agriculture, Westmoreland County experienced a 10% decline in the total number of farms between 2017 and 2022, dropping from 1,099 to 989 farms, even as total farmland fell only about 4%.

Easements like Tomlinson’s are one way landowners have responded. The Western Pennsylvania Conservancy says it has permanently protected more than 30,000 acres in the Ligonier Valley since the 1970s, more than 12,000 of them through easements.
Negotiating which rights to restrict

Easement terms are negotiated property by property. In my family’s negotiations, we have had to work out what we and future owners can still do with the ranch. We have agreed to limit where future buildings can go, to permanently restrict the use of certain pesticides and to prohibit new roads and stream crossings.
Other easements may allow different agricultural, forestry or construction activities, depending on their terms.

Reaching agreement can be expensive. Natural Lands, a Pennsylvania land trust, lists typical transaction costs. These include surveys, appraisals, environmental assessments, legal fees, title work and documentation of the property’s existing condition. The cost to negotiate my family’s easement has run well into six figures.

Once an easement is signed, the holder is responsible for monitoring and enforcing it for as long as it lasts. Land trusts commonly ask landowners for stewardship funding to help pay for that future work.
The land trust that holds our easement will work with whoever owns the land after us, not just with us, so choosing the right partner was an important part of our decision.
How conservation is financed
Beyond transaction costs, granting an easement usually lowers a property’s market value.

To see how this works, imagine the hypothetical farm is worth $4 million with its development rights and $2 million once an easement sharply restricts subdividing it. (These figures are for illustration; how much an easement lowers a property’s value varies widely with its location, development potential and the restrictions involved.) Appraisers often value an easement by comparing a property’s value before and after it’s placed on the land. Here, the easement would be worth $2 million: the amount it cuts from the property’s value.
To encourage landowners to grant easements, U.S. tax law allows a charitable deduction for donated easements that meet detailed requirements. Easements can also be sold.

In Tomlinson’s case, private foundation grants paid for the conservancy’s purchase. Government programs offer another route: The U.S. Department of Agriculture helps eligible organizations, such as land trusts and state and local governments, to buy easements on farmland. These payments and tax benefits can help landowners absorb the drop in property value. For the public, buying or subsidizing easements can protect more land per dollar than buying land outright.
Tax benefits and tax abuse
The tax breaks tied to easements have also invited abuse.

The Internal Revenue Service has identified inflated appraisals and improperly large charitable deductions as recurring problems. A 2019 report by the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that some promoters sold investors stakes in partnerships and similar entities that then donated easements at inflated values. When appraisals exaggerate a property’s development potential, investors can claim deductions based on those inflated values.
Congress later restricted deductions for certain conservation contributions by partnerships and corporations. Courts have also disallowed deductions and imposed penalties in abusive transactions.
What it means to protect land forever
To qualify for the federal charitable deduction, a donated easement must protect the land permanently.

Property scholar Gerald Korngold of New York Law School has argued that the permanence that makes easements attractive also makes them hard to adjust and that changing ecological conditions and competing community needs can create reasons to revisit restrictions.

In one case Korngold describes, a conservation easement in Vermont blocked the federal government from adding the land to a national wildlife refuge – a move every party supported – because federal rules require clear title.

I have taught property law for decades and have written about the challenges of private land conservation for much of that time. These experiences taught me that an easement has to address two things: what to protect and what happens if circumstances change.

Negotiating one for my family’s ranch made that, and the bundle of sticks metaphor, real for me. We had to write language setting the dimensions of the particular sticks my grandchildren will live with, under conditions none of us can predict.

Done properly, a conservation easement leaves room for land use to adapt without undermining its conservation goals. It lets landowners like Tomlinson’s family and mine protect land while keeping it in private hands.
Andrew P. Morriss is affiliated with Property and Environment Research Center (PERC).

articles.title: Thanksgiving dinner is likely to be served with a side of political disagreement
articles.author: Matthew W. Kreuter, Kahn Family Professor of Public Health, Washington University in St. Louis
paras: Every year as Thanksgiving approaches, news stories are written about how holiday gatherings bring together people who see the world very differently, sometimes leading to uncomfortable dinner conversations. The stories usually include advice about avoiding awkward moments and topics that are off-limits, and navigating heated conversations if they arise.

As experts in health communication and public health, we are keenly aware of how conversations with family members and close friends shape people’s decisions and actions and that sometimes the benefits of having difficult conversations outweigh the potential costs. We wondered how often difficult conversations actually take place at Thanksgiving meals and what the conversations are about.

Although studies have demonstrated that Thanksgiving meals involving people with diverse political viewpoints were shorter by 24 minutes than meals among people holding similar views, we found no estimates of how often these conversations occur.

Our survey of 354 adults from 17 states found that over half – 57% – will share a Thanksgiving meal this year with at least one person from outside their household who sees the world very differently than they do. In 4 out of 5 of these cases, the way their viewpoints differ is politics.

The survey participants were initially recruited to represent differing perspectives on health; they were not randomly selected to represent the general population. That means the survey’s findings may not be generalizable beyond the study sample.
Table talk: What do Americans expect this Thanksgiving?

From Nov. 7-9, 2026, we surveyed 354 adults from 17 states about their plans for this year’s Thanksgiving. Respondents were part of an ongoing health knowledge monitoring and response system. Their mean age was 47.1 years; three-quarters of them were women; and they were racially and ethnically diverse, with 44% white, 33% African American, 15% Hispanic ethnicity and 8% another race or ethnicity. About 1 in 10 were rural residents, and 43% had children under 18 living in their home.
The questions about Thanksgiving meals were sent to 430 people on Nov. 7; 354 completed a survey, which is an 82% response rate.
Of the 354 respondents, 80% expected to share a meal with family members or friends from outside their household during the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday.

Those planning to share a meal with others from outside their household were then asked, “Holiday meals sometimes bring together people from different generations, with different views, or different life experiences. Thinking about your upcoming Thanksgiving meal, will anyone be there who sees the world very differently than you do?”
Almost 71% of those planning to share a meal with others outside their household said yes.

Asked “What are those differences about?” by far the most common response was politics, at 81%, followed by religion at almost 58%, differing views about people such as their career choices or relationships at 54%, health at 53%; and half of the respondents said money. A few mentioned other differences such as “raising children” and “parenting” and “gender expression” and “LGBTQ.”

Asked if they think any of those differences will be expressed during the meal, almost 60% said yes. This was especially true for differences in politics. A large majority – 79% – of respondents said that differences in politics would be expressed during the meal. Fewer respondents – 40% or less – expected that differences in views about people, money, religion or health would be expressed.
Then our questions got to who is expected to disagree – and what respondents anticipate the disagreements will be about. These responses varied by race and ethnicity.

White respondents were more likely than African American or Hispanic respondents to say that others at their Thanksgiving meal will view politics differently from them. African American respondents were more likely than White or Hispanic respondents to say that others at their meal will view money matters differently and were more likely than Hispanics to say that others at their meal will view certain people differently.

In short, it’s highly common for those gathered around any Thanksgiving table this year to have different views on key matters, but the differences you’re most likely to hear about during mealtime conversation are political.

Science tells us that conflict resolution improves through dialogue by reducing stereotypes and changing attitudes that tend to divide people. Holiday meals could provide some clues about how Americans navigate conversations with those who hold different viewpoints from them on politics, religion, money and health.
As one panel member commented: “I don’t keep people around just because they agree with me on something. I don’t cut people away because we disagree about something.”
Tori De La Vega contributed to this story.
